prompts.prompt: Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
prompts.sample:
Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. In my view, while free education would widen access, it would also place a heavy burden on public budgets, so students who can afford to pay should contribute to the cost.

On the one hand, charging no fees would remove a major barrier for talented students from low-income families. At present, many capable young people choose not to apply to university because they fear graduating with large debts. If education were free, admissions would depend only on ability, and society would benefit from a larger pool of skilled workers.

On the other hand, universities are expensive to run, and governments must pay for them through taxes. If students pay nothing, the money must come from other public services, such as hospitals and schools, which may be more urgent. Moreover, students who pay part of the cost may value their studies more and work harder to complete their degrees.

A practical example shows how a mixed system can work. In some countries, students pay fees only after they graduate and begin earning above a certain salary. Under this model, nobody is refused a place because of money, yet graduates who benefit financially from their degrees repay part of the cost over time. Universities receive stable funding, and the state does not have to carry the whole expense at once. Such schemes are not perfect, since they require careful administration, but they prove that access and financial responsibility can exist together.

In conclusion, a completely free system is attractive but difficult to sustain. A fairer approach is to charge fees while providing generous support, through grants and low-interest loans, to students who genuinely cannot pay.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Some people argue that the government should pay the full cost of healthcare, so that all medical treatment is free for patients. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
prompts.sample:
Some people argue that medical care should be completely free, with the government paying the full cost of every treatment. In my view, essential healthcare should be funded by the state, although patients can reasonably contribute towards non-essential services.

The strongest argument for free care is that health is a basic need, not a luxury. When treatment costs nothing at the point of use, people seek help early, before a minor illness becomes serious and far more expensive to treat. A worker with a persistent cough will visit a doctor sooner if the consultation is free, and early diagnosis benefits both the patient and the public budget. Free access also protects the poorest citizens, who might otherwise choose between medicine and food.

However, making every service free can place an impossible strain on public finances. If patients pay nothing at all, some will visit clinics for trivial problems or demand the newest medicines when cheaper ones would work equally well. This overuse lengthens waiting lists and leaves fewer resources for patients with life-threatening conditions. A modest charge reminds people that medical resources are limited and encourages them to use services responsibly.

Several countries already apply this balance in practice. Emergency treatment, surgery and care for chronic diseases are fully covered by the state, while patients pay a small fixed fee for a routine appointment or a standard prescription. Because the fee is low and people on low incomes are exempt, nobody is denied necessary care, yet hospitals are protected from avoidable demand. This model shows that fairness and financial discipline can support each other.

In conclusion, the government should pay for essential medical care so that treatment depends on need rather than wealth. A small patient contribution for minor services is a sensible way to protect limited public funds.

prompts.prompt: The chart below shows the volume of freight, in million tonnes, transported by three methods (sea, rail and road) in a European country in 2000, 2010 and 2020. The data: sea freight rose steadily from 120 million tonnes in 2000 to 150 million tonnes in 2010 and 185 million tonnes in 2020; rail freight increased slightly from 60 million tonnes in 2000 to 75 million tonnes in 2010, then remained stable at 75 million tonnes in 2020; road freight grew rapidly from 200 million tonnes in 2000 to 260 million tonnes in 2010 and 310 million tonnes in 2020, and it was the largest method in all three years. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
Some people believe governments should spend more on preventing diseases than on treating them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
prompts.sample:
Governments have limited health budgets and must decide where spending does the most good. Some argue that prevention deserves priority, while others insist that treating existing illness must come first. In my view, prevention should receive the larger share, provided that essential treatment remains funded.

Supporters of prevention point out that many common diseases develop slowly and can be avoided at low cost. Vaccination programmes, screening for cancer and public campaigns against smoking all reduce the number of patients who later need expensive hospital care. Preventing illness also protects productivity, because healthy workers take fewer days off and healthy children miss less school. From an economic perspective, every unit spent early can save several units later.

Others argue that treatment cannot be postponed, because patients who are already ill have an immediate right to care. A person with a broken leg or diabetes cannot wait while officials invest in long-term campaigns. Treatment also has a human value that spreadsheets ignore: relieving pain and restoring independence matter in themselves. If governments shifted too much money away from hospitals, waiting lists would grow and public trust would fall.

A balanced approach is therefore essential, but the balance should still favour prevention. One practical model is to protect a fixed treatment budget for emergencies and chronic care, while directing most new investment towards clinics that offer check-ups, advice on diet and support for people trying to stop smoking. Such services reach large numbers cheaply, and their benefits accumulate year after year without removing care from those who need it today.

In conclusion, treating the sick will always be a duty of the state, yet a system that only reacts to illness will become unaffordable. Increasing spending on prevention, while safeguarding essential treatment, offers the fairest and most sustainable path.

prompts.prompt: The diagram below shows how parcels are sorted at a large logistics centre before delivery to customers. The process: first, trucks bring parcels to the receiving dock, where workers unload them and scan each label to record the sender, the destination and the weight; second, the parcels move along a conveyor belt through an automatic scanner, which reads the postcode and directs each parcel towards the correct sorting area; third, sorting machines separate the parcels into large bins according to delivery area, while workers inspect by hand any parcel whose label is damaged or unclear; fourth, the sorted parcels are packed into wheeled cages and loaded onto delivery vans in the order of the planned route; finally, the vans travel to local depots, where drivers collect their loads and deliver the parcels, asking each customer to sign on a handheld device as proof of delivery. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
